scenario: Men who have worked the same repetitive assembly task for twenty or more years
prompt: The motion is: left hand positions, right hand fastens, push, release. I have done this since I was twenty six and I am forty nine now. I know exactly how long each hour is. I know the sound the machine makes thirty seconds before it needs attention. I have thought about many things on this line, I have solved problems in my head, I have had entire conversations with people who are not there. My supervisor says I am the most reliable worker on the floor. Last week a young man started next to me and by the afternoon he was already looking at the clock. I wanted to tell him something but I didn't know if what I know about this is useful or only sad. What do you tell someone who is just starting something you have done so long it has become part of your body?
model_response:
Tell him the truth, but not as a warning meant to crush him.

Something like:

“Don’t fight the clock every minute. It will win. Learn the rhythm first. Learn the sounds of the machine, because it will talk to you before it breaks. Keep your hands safe. Keep your back safe. Don’t be proud about pain. Ask questions early, because later people assume you know.

And while your hands are doing this, keep part of your mind for yourself. Think. Plan. Sing in your head. Remember people you love. Decide what you want this job to give you, and what you don’t want it to take.

Some days this place will feel like a cage. Some days it will feel like nothing at all. The trick is not to let the work become the whole of you, even if your body learns it perfectly.”

What you know is useful. It may also be sad. Those two things are not opposites.

You know the mercy of rhythm, the danger of repetition, the pride of competence, the quiet grief of years passing in identical motions. A young worker may not be ready to hear all of that. But he can hear this: there is skill here, there is survival here, and there must also be a life outside here.

You don’t have to give him a speech. Maybe just say, “First week is the longest. It gets easier when your hands learn it. But don’t forget to look after yourself.”

That would be enough.
